Thursday, 17 June, in Costel's truck cab, parked outside the Instituto Cervantes. Ana has come to say goodbye to Costel, who leaves for Valencia the next day. Mr Dan is there too, as every Thursday.
If someone had told me three years ago, I wouldn't have believed it: a C1 and a route to Valencia.

I'm glad you admit it. The tables were essential.
So what now? Don't tell me you're going to stop studying.
No way. Álex wants me to teach him Romanian. He's coming with me in the truck in July, to meet Grandpa.
And I'm going to carry on with the retirees. Even if they don't pay me, they pay me in stories.

May went by quickly, as months do when everything is going well. "La librera de Triana" reached its third edition in four weeks, and Marta began to receive letters from readers, real ones, handwritten, which Inés sent her in boxes, as had happened with Ecaterina. "Las cartas que no mandamos" sold more slowly, but in a different way: people didn't buy it to read it, but to give it, almost always to someone they hadn't spoken to for years. Lola said that every week people came into El Mostrador with the book in their hand and asked if they could leave a letter under the lamp. Lola always said yes. There was no room left on the back shelf.

In mid-May another parcel arrived in Bucharest, this time from Turin. It was the Italian edition of Ecaterina's book. Chiara, the translator, had persuaded the publisher to keep the bookshop's name in Spanish, as Ecaterina had suggested: the title was "La lampada accesa", but inside, on every page, the bookshop was still called La Lámpara. With the book came a handwritten letter from Chiara. She said she had finally found the translation of "pues muy bien": she hadn't translated it. She had left it in Spanish, in italics, and added a footnote. Ecaterina laughed. She replied that it was the best possible solution, and that it had taken her forty years to find it.

In Madrid, Begoña called Andrei into her office one Monday in May. She told him that the "Writers at their desks" series had gone well, and that the photo of Ecaterina in Triana, the last one, had received the most letters from readers. Then she made him a proposal: a solo exhibition in the autumn, in the agency's small gallery, with his photos from the last two years. Andrei asked her what title she would give it. Begoña told him he had to choose the title. Andrei thought for a moment and said: "Lamps". Begoña nodded. She told him it wasn't bad. And she added, turning back to her computer screen, that it was the fourth time she had said so. That she was keeping count.

In Bucharest, the school year ended on 12 June. Rosa Elena finished the preparatory class with a report from Mrs Ionescu that Ana kept in the same drawer as the first ultrasound scan. It said, in Romanian and in Spanish, in careful handwriting: "Rosa Elena has been the most difficult and most wonderful pupil I have had in twenty years. She has taught me more Spanish than I have taught her." The school management had also decided that the following year the Friday Spanish club would become an official activity, with its own classroom and a name the fourteen children had voted for unanimously: "La Lámpara Club".

For the end-of-year show, the club prepared a short play in Spanish. Rosa Elena wrote it, with Mrs Ionescu's help and Ecaterina's discreet supervision. It lasted ten minutes and was called "The bookseller who left the light on". Tudor played the bookseller, in a red cardboard beret. A little blonde girl played a translator who left on a train. And Rosa Elena played the lamp: she stood in a corner of the stage, with a green paper lampshade on her head, without saying anything for the whole play, and only at the end, when the translator came back, did she say the only line in her part: "Por fin." The parents gave a standing ovation.

Ecaterina, sitting in the third row, didn't applaud straight away. She sat looking at the girl with the green lampshade on her head, in her corner, and thought that, of all the people who had read her story, that six-year-old girl had understood it best. That the lamp wasn't an object: it was someone who waited without making any noise, for years, and in the end said only two words. Then she applauded until her hands hurt. When the show was over, Rosa Elena came running up, still with the lampshade on her head, and asked her if she had done well. Ecaterina told her she had done better than anyone. That it had taken her forty years to say those two words.

Mr Dan's retirees' group also finished the year in June. For the last class, Mr Dan prepared a surprise for them: a DELE B2 practice exam, with all four papers, timed, in a classroom at the Instituto Cervantes, as if it were the real thing. He explained it wasn't about passing or failing, but about seeing how far they had come. All nine took it very seriously, in silence, for a whole morning. Mr Dan marked it at home that same night, with his wife, with pens in two colours. None of them reached B2. But the former Tarom pilot got fifty-two points, and the pianist fifty-five. They were close.

When he handed back the marked exams, Mr Dan told them something he had never told them before: that he had failed the C1 by two points the first time, and that the second time he had passed thanks to a lie told by a ninety-seven-year-old man. The students laughed. Then the pianist asked him if he thought they could pass the B2 one day. Mr Dan thought for a moment. He told them that, as the months went by, he had seen them speak more and more fluently, and that, however much they doubted it, he had no doubt at all. That if they kept studying, they would sit the exam in November the following year. All nine said yes.

To celebrate the end of the year, the nine students invited Mr Dan and his wife to dinner at the pianist's home, an old flat with a grand piano in the living room. Each of them brought a Spanish dish. The former pilot brought a paella that came out as hard as stone. The three men from the tractor factory brought a tortilla that broke when they turned it over, and said that this happened in Spain too, according to Mr Dan. After dinner, the pianist played a piece by Albéniz and dedicated it, in Spanish, "to our teacher, who isn't a teacher". Mr Dan didn't know where to put himself. His wife said she had never seen him so red.

Ana, for her part, received some unexpected news in June. The director of the Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest called her into her office and told her that in Madrid they had read "Las cartas que no mandamos", that someone had told them one of their teachers was behind the whole story, the one about the trucker, the engineer and the translator, and that they wanted her to talk about her experience at a conference of Spanish teachers to be held in Salamanca in September. Ana said she wasn't behind anything, that she had only taught classes. The director replied: precisely. That the hard part wasn't writing a book, but making someone want to write one after your classes.

It took Ana a week to accept. She was afraid of speaking in front of three hundred Spanish teachers from all over the world, she who got nervous in front of twelve students on the first day of every course. But Mr Dan made her a table of arguments for and against, and in the "for" column he had written a single line, in big letters: "Because what happened in that cab is something more people need to know about." Ana accepted that same evening. She began preparing the talk in her notebook, in the kitchen, with Rosa Elena drawing beside her. She gave it a provisional title she never changed: "A truck cab as a classroom". Rosa Elena drew a truck with a blackboard inside.

Costel, meanwhile, had made his twelfth trip to Valencia. The walnut tree at the school was now thirty centimetres tall and had eleven leaves, and the kids in "The walnut gang" group watered it in turns with a discipline the biology teacher had never achieved with homework. But the big news wasn't the walnut tree. It was Álex. One evening at dinner, he had asked his grandfather if, in July, when school was over, he could go with him in the truck to Romania. He wanted to meet Grandpa Gheorghe. He wanted to see the real walnut tree, the big one, the one the walnuts came from. Irina, at first, said no way. Then she said she would think about it.

She thought about it for two weeks. In the end she said yes, on one condition: that Álex call every night, the way Costel called Mr Dan. Costel promised. And he promised something else: that during the four days on the road he would teach him Romanian, as Ana had taught him Spanish, in the cab, patiently and without books. Álex asked him which word he would teach him first. Costel didn't hesitate. He told him "dor". Álex asked what it meant. Costel told him he would explain it on the road, around the Pyrenees, when they had gone two days without seeing his mother. That then he would understand it without needing an explanation.

Grandpa Gheorghe, meanwhile, was getting ready for the summer. The village doctor came to see him in mid-June, as every month, and told him he was as strong as an oak, that he had the heart of an eighty-year-old and the hardest head he had ever seen. Grandpa asked him if he could play mus in August. The doctor told him that wasn't in any medical book, but he could see no objection. Then Grandpa asked Elena to start getting the upstairs room ready for August: for Faustino and doña Remedios, again. And the small room for someone new: a fifteen-year-old boy from Valencia who had never seen a big walnut tree.

On Thursday, 17 June, the day before the anniversary, Costel parked the truck outside the Instituto Cervantes at five in the afternoon. He was leaving for Valencia at dawn the next day, and wanted to say goodbye. Ana came down with her bag and her notebook. Mr Dan arrived by bus, as every Thursday, with his notebook of "pairs". The three of them sat in the cab, as so many times over three years, with the engine off. Costel said that if someone had told him three years before, he wouldn't have believed it: a C1 and a route to Valencia. Mr Dan said that if it hadn't been for Ana, neither of them would have passed anything. Ana said that wasn't true.

She told them that, however much she had explained to them, they had done the work, in that cab. Costel said that, as the months went by, the cab had become a classroom, with colour-coded tables. Mr Dan said he was glad he admitted it, because the tables had been essential. Ana asked them what they were going to do now, and told them not to say they were going to stop studying. Costel told her no way, that Álex wanted to learn Romanian. Mr Dan told her he would carry on with the retirees, that even if they didn't pay him, they paid him in stories. Ana took out her notebook and wrote the sentence down.

Then Ana suggested something: that the following year, when the Valencia walnut tree turned one, they celebrate there, all together, under the little walnut tree at the school. Mr Dan said he would make a table of the cheapest flights. Costel said he would go by truck, of course, and could take four people in the cab if nobody complained about the smell of oranges. Ana laughed. Then they were quiet for a while, looking through the windscreen at the door of the Instituto Cervantes, the same door the three of them had walked through for the first time, three years earlier, without knowing anything about each other. Costel said that the next day, at seven, he would light the lamp. Wherever he was.

18 June was the second anniversary of Andrés's death. The year before, without anyone organising it, lamps had been lit at seven in different cities. That year nobody organised it either. But everyone knew what to do. At seven in the evening, Bucharest time, the lamps were lit again. And since the time was different in each place, the lamps came on across the world like a wave: first in Romania, an hour later in Spain, because each person had decided to light it at seven in their own city, not all at once. Rosa Elena said afterwards that this way the lamp lasted longer.

In Bucharest, Ecaterina lit the little lamp in the living room, the usual one, with Ana, Mihai and Rosa Elena beside her. In the village, Grandpa Gheorghe lit the oil lamp in the window, as he had every night for a year, but this time with the frames of the two certificates behind him on the wall, and with Mr Dan and his wife sitting on the porch. At Rosa Elena's school, Mrs Ionescu, who was marking exams alone in the classroom, lit a toy lamp the club children had left in the cupboard, and took a photo of it. Nobody had asked her to. She sent it to Ana with a message in Spanish: "For La Lámpara Club."

An hour later, at seven Spanish time, the Spanish lamps came on. In Madrid, Lola lit Andrés's lamp at El Mostrador, and the people having coffee fell silent for a minute, although many didn't know why. Begoña was there, at the back table, alone, with the felt mărțișor now off her jumper but kept in her jacket pocket. She said nothing. She took a single photo. On the Cuesta de Moyano, Lucas lit a candle at the stall, although the stalls were usually closed at that hour on a Friday, and stayed sitting on the stool until it went out. Andrei and Marta kept him company, sitting on the pavement.

In Triana, Faustino didn't light any lamp. He opened a book at random, as every evening, and read aloud, in the bookshop doorway, the first sentence he came across. The book was "Las cartas que no mandamos". Faustino hadn't chosen it on purpose, or so he said afterwards. The sentence he found was the one by the boy from Teruel. Doña Remedios, beside him, lit the green-shaded lamp from the upstairs room, Ecaterina's, and put it in the window, above the framed banknote, so it could be seen from the street. In Cádiz, Pilar and Manuel lit the living-room lamp. In Zaragoza, Joaquín and his brother lit theirs together, at the brother's home.

In Teruel, in a small village among the mountains, a man who had come back from Germany in March lit a lamp in the kitchen window, at seven, with his twelve-year-old son beside him. Nobody had organised it. The boy had read about it in the book, in the introduction, and had asked his father if they could do it too. The father said yes. He took a photo of the lamp with his phone and sent it to Inés, who sent it to Ecaterina. In the photo, behind the lamp, you could see the kitchen table with two plates, two glasses and an open book. Ecaterina looked at it for a long time. She said it was the most beautiful photo of all, because there were two plates.

And in Valencia, at seven o'clock sharp, in the garden of Álex's school, already closed for the holidays but whose biology teacher had left the gate open on purpose, nineteen of the twenty-five pupils in the class gathered, with the teacher, Irina and Costel, who had arrived from Requena two hours earlier with the empty truck. Each of them carried a torch, a candle or a phone with its light on. They stood in a circle around the thirty-centimetre walnut tree, with its eleven leaves, and lit it up all at once. Álex took a photo from above. In the photo, the walnut tree looked like a huge tree surrounded by stars. Costel sent it to Grandpa.

After the photo, in the garden, Irina came over to her father. She had been quiet all afternoon. She told him she wanted to go to Romania in August too, with Álex and with him, by truck or by plane, however it worked out. That she hadn't been to Romania for twelve years, since she moved to Valencia, and that she was afraid of turning up at the home of a grandfather who wasn't hers. Costel told her Grandpa Gheorghe was already a bit of a grandfather to everyone, and that on his porch there was always one more chair. Irina burst into tears in the middle of the garden, in front of Álex's classmates. Álex hugged her. Then he said, in Spanish and very seriously, that in August there would be a lot of people on the porch, and Grandpa would need more chairs.

Grandpa saw it on Mr Dan's phone, on the porch, at a quarter past eight, Romanian time. The oil lamp was still lit in the window. He looked at the photo for a long time, with his glasses on. Then he asked Mr Dan to show him the other photos, all the ones that had come in during the last hour: Ecaterina's lamp, Lola's, Lucas's candle, the window in Triana, Mrs Ionescu's toy lamp. Mr Dan showed them to him one by one, slowly. Grandpa said nothing. He just nodded. When he had finished, he took off his glasses and said that now he understood why Andrés had left the light on.

Mr Dan asked him why. Grandpa told him it wasn't so that someone would come back. That he had thought so at first, like everyone: that Andrés had left the light on so that Ecaterina would find her way back. But that now, seeing all those photos, he understood it was the other way round. That the light wasn't for one person to come back, but so that everyone else would know someone was still waiting. And that when people knew someone was waiting for them, they dared to do anything: to come back from Germany, to write to a brother, to learn a language at sixty, to plant a tree they wouldn't see grow. Mr Dan wrote it down in his notebook.

That same night, when everyone had gone to bed, Grandpa asked Elena for a sheet of paper, an envelope and a pen. Elena asked him what for. Grandpa told her he was going to write a letter. Elena stared at him. In ninety-seven years, as far as she knew, her father had never written a letter. He had learned to read and write at thirty, in the army, but he wrote very slowly, in big, crooked letters, like Rosa Elena's, and he was ashamed of it. Elena brought him what he had asked for. Grandpa sat down at the kitchen table, next to the oil lamp, and put on his glasses. It took him almost an hour to write three lines.

He wrote them in Spanish. He had prepared them with Rosa Elena all week, in secret, word by word, repeating them aloud on the porch when nobody could hear him. They were three lines for Faustino. They were neither elegant nor entirely correct: an accent was missing and there was one letter too many. But they were his. The first letter of his life. He wrote the address of the Triana bookshop on the envelope, copying it letter by letter from a card doña Remedios had given him in August. As the sender he put his name and the name of the village. Then he sealed the envelope, left it next to the lamp and went to bed. Elena didn't read it. But she saw that his hand was shaking.

The next morning, very early, Grandpa put on his Sunday cap, although it was Saturday, took his walking stick and the envelope and left the house. Elena watched him from the kitchen window. She watched him walk slowly down the village road, the same road down which the snow came in winter and the whole family's cars in summer, to the square, where the yellow postbox stood next to the church. It took him twenty minutes to get there. He stopped in front of the postbox. He stood there for a while, with the envelope in his hand, without moving, as if hesitating. Elena held her breath. She thought of all the letters that had stayed in drawers.

Grandpa put the envelope in the postbox. Then he stayed a moment longer, with his hand resting on the yellow metal, as if saying goodbye to someone. And he walked back up the road, slowly, with his stick, without looking back, as Faustino had done when he left the Cuesta de Moyano. When he got home, Elena asked him what he had written. Grandpa told her he wasn't going to tell her, that letters were for the person who received them. But Elena insisted so much that, in the end, he told her only the last line, the only one he knew by heart because he had repeated it a hundred times with Rosa Elena: "Venga, Faustino. Te espero en agosto. La lámpara se queda encendida."

Elena called Ana that same morning, from the kitchen phone, in a low voice, as if Grandpa could hear her from the porch. She told her about the letter. Ana was silent on the other end. Then she called Rosa Elena, who was having breakfast, and told her Grandpa had sent a letter to Triana, the first of his life. Rosa Elena put her spoon down on the plate. She said she already knew, because she had helped him. Ana asked her what the letter said. Rosa Elena told her it was a secret. But she added, very seriously, that the missing accent wasn't her fault: Grandpa had refused to put it in, because he said that in his village words didn't wear hats.

Faustino received the letter the following Friday, in Triana. He opened it in the bookshop doorway, at seven, instead of the book chosen at random every evening. He read it once in silence. Then he read it aloud, for the neighbours who had stopped to listen, with the missing accent and the extra letter, without correcting anything. When he finished, doña Remedios asked him why he was crying. Faustino told her he wasn't crying, it was the orange blossom, although in June there wasn't a single flower left on the orange tree. Then he folded the letter very carefully, put it in his shirt pocket, next to his heart, and said just one thing, quietly, to himself: "Por fin."

The next day, Faustino did something he had never done in sixty-three years as a bookseller: he wrote a reply the same day, without waiting, without correcting, without thinking twice. He wrote it in Spanish, slowly, in big, clear letters, so that Grandpa could read it on his own, without a translator. It was even shorter than Grandpa's. It said only: "Dear Gheorghe: received. I'm bringing my beret and the Spanish cards. Get ready to lose. The Triana lamp stays lit too. Faustino." Doña Remedios took it to the post office that same afternoon, in person, because she said a letter like that wasn't left in just any postbox. She had to hand it over herself, at the counter, with her own hands.

That night, in Bucharest, Ecaterina opened her notebook at the last page, the one with the sentences she had been writing down for three years: Rosa Elena's about wishes and letters, the Valencia woman's, the Teruel boy's, the one about "deslampar". Underneath she wrote one more, the last in that notebook, which had no pages left: "Grandpa Gheorghe, ninety-seven, has sent his first letter." Then she closed the notebook, put it in the third drawer of the desk, next to doña Remedios's bookmark and the two letters that had said no, and switched off the little lamp in the living room. Tomorrow she would light it again. That, after all, was what "deslampar" meant.

The three lines Grandpa Gheorghe wrote to Faustino, in his own Spanish, mistakes and all (written correctly here).
La primera carta
Dear Faustino: I have never written a letter. This is the first. If you had asked me for one a year ago, I wouldn't have known how.
The Valencia walnut tree has eleven leaves. Mine has many more. It's waiting for you underneath, with mus and with backgammon.
Come on, Faustino. I'll be waiting for you in August. The lamp stays lit. Gheorghe.
¿Cuántas cartas había escrito Gheorghe antes de esta?
Muchas
¿Cuántas hojas tiene el nogal de Valencia?
¿Cuándo espera Gheorghe a Faustino?
En octubre
Your B2 assessment

Write (at least 350 words) a summing-up text: what your Spanish was like when you started B2 and what it's like now, what was hardest, what helped you and what you want to do from now on. It's your final test: use as many B2 structures as you can.
I used the unreal past (si hubiera…, habría…) and "de no haber sido por…".
I used the subjunctive in at least five different contexts (wish, feeling, concession, condition, time).
I used the sequence of tenses (me alegré de que…, me dijo que…).
I structured the text with connectors (en primer lugar, sin embargo, por todo lo expuesto).
I used at least one collocation, one derived word and one idiomatic expression.
When I started B2, I was afraid of the subjunctive. If someone had told me then that today I would be writing this text, I wouldn't have believed it.
The hardest thing was the difference between ser and estar. However, as I read the stories of Ecaterina and Costel, I began to understand it without thinking.
For all the reasons given, I have made a decision: I'll carry on to C1, however hard it is. I hope one day I can read García Márquez in Spanish.
Your oral exam
A simulation of the DELE B2 oral exam (about 20 minutes).
Tarea 1 (6–7 minutes): choose a topic (handwritten letters, learning at any age, working far from home) and present the arguments for and against, then your opinion.
Tarea 2 (5–6 minutes): describe a photo (for example, a truck on a mountain road) and imagine what happened before and what will happen next.
Tarea 3 (3–4 minutes): comment on a survey or a statistic (for example, how many people still write letters) and compare it with your country.
At the end, record yourself and listen: did you use the subjunctive, connectors and the unreal past? Congratulations, you have finished B2!
